title: Ancient Egyptian heka and amuletic practice
publicDomainBasis: The ancient practices and artifacts are public-domain historical subject matter. Wiccan uses independently written factual summaries and does not reproduce copyrighted modern translations or museum prose.
sourceReference: British Museum, 'Heka: magic in ancient Egypt'; Metropolitan Museum of Art, 'Ancient Egyptian Amulets'. https://www.metmuseum.org/essays/egyptian-amulets
summary: Ancient Egyptian magical practice, commonly discussed through the concept of heka, was integrated with religion and everyday concerns. Amulets were widely used, and their intended efficacy could depend on form, material, color, inscription, spoken words, and ritual action.
groundedFacts: Heka was treated in ancient Egypt as a power woven into religious life and was used in contexts including protection, health, justice, childbirth, and the afterlife.
Amulets were used across a very long span of Egyptian history and could be worn by the living or placed with the dead.
The intended magical significance of an amulet could derive from its shape, decoration, inscription, color, material, words spoken over it, or actions performed with it.
Textual amulets could consist of short magical texts written on linen or papyrus, folded, and worn on a string.
Modern lessons must describe these beliefs historically and must not present amulets as scientifically proven protection or medical treatment.

title: Maqlû anti-witchcraft incantation and ritual series
period: Ancient Mesopotamia; first-millennium BCE manuscript tradition
publicDomainBasis: The ancient cuneiform source tradition is public-domain historical subject matter. Wiccan uses independently written summaries and does not reproduce modern copyrighted translations.
sourceReference: ORACC Corpus of Mesopotamian Anti-witchcraft Rituals (CMAwR), Maqlû ritual tablets including Q002713 and related ritual texts. https://oracc.museum.upenn.edu/cmawro/corpus
summary: Maqlû is an ancient Mesopotamian anti-witchcraft ritual and incantation tradition. Surviving ritual tablets combine spoken incantations with symbolic actions such as work with figurines, fire, washing or purification, and appeals to divine powers including Šamaš and Girra.
groundedFacts: Maqlû is preserved as a Mesopotamian incantation-and-ritual series concerned with undoing perceived witchcraft.
The ritual tablet includes instructions accompanying recited incantations and purification actions.
Related Maqlû ritual texts attest the burning of figurines as a symbolic action in rites intended to counter witchcraft.
Some rites invoke deities such as Šamaš and Girra in judicial, purifying, or destructive symbolic roles.
These texts reflect ancient Mesopotamian religious and ritual assumptions; they must not be presented as modern Wicca or as evidence that accusations of witchcraft were objectively true.
Descriptions of burning, illness, or hostile magic are historical material only and must not be converted into instructions for harming people or property.

title: London-Leiden Demotic Magical Papyrus
publicDomainBasis: The ancient papyrus is public-domain historical subject matter. Wiccan uses independently written summaries and does not reproduce copyrighted modern translations.
sourceReference: British Museum EA10070; P. Leiden/London, commonly catalogued as PDM XIV. https://www.britishmuseum.org/collection/object/Y_EA10070-1
summary: The London-Leiden papyrus preserves a Roman-period Egyptian collection of spells, ritual recipes, invocations, and divinatory procedures written mainly in Demotic, with Old Coptic glosses and Greek recitation. It is evidence for the multilingual and syncretic ritual culture of late antique Egypt.
groundedFacts: The surviving papyrus is dated to the early third century CE and is associated with Thebes in Egypt.
Its text includes spells and ritual recipes as well as procedures for divination and invocations.
The manuscript is primarily Demotic and also contains Old Coptic glosses and Greek recitation, showing a multilingual ritual environment.
The collection includes material concerning healing, love, divination, and other aims, but some historical recipes are unsafe by modern standards.
Lessons may discuss the manuscript's historical contents and cultural setting but must not turn poisonous, coercive, or medical recipes into modern instructions.
The papyrus belongs to a syncretic late-antique Egyptian context and must not be described as an ancient Wiccan text.

title: Harris Magical Papyrus
publicDomainBasis: The ancient papyrus is public-domain historical subject matter. Wiccan uses independently written summaries and does not reproduce copyrighted modern translations.
sourceReference: British Museum EA10042, the Harris Magical Papyrus. https://www.britishmuseum.org/collection/object/Y_EA10042-1
summary: The Harris Magical Papyrus is a New Kingdom Egyptian magical manuscript preserving a collection of hymns and incantations. It provides direct evidence that written ritual literature could combine devotional language and protective or magical speech in ancient Egypt.
groundedFacts: The Harris Magical Papyrus is an ancient Egyptian manuscript from the New Kingdom.
The surviving material contains magical text described as a collection of hymns and incantations.
Its existence demonstrates that ritual and magical speech could be preserved in written papyrus collections.
A lesson may discuss the coexistence of hymn, invocation, and incantation as categories of ritual language without inventing lost wording or ritual steps.
The manuscript must be presented as ancient Egyptian material, not as evidence of an ancient Wiccan lineage.
